newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Christians vow to keep the faith under Beijing.
newsitem.headline: HK Christians vow to keep the faith under Beijing.

text.p: God or country? Half a million Chinese Christians in Hong Kong pray they won't face such a choice when Britain hands the territory back to China on July 1.
"We are Christians, but we are also Chinese proud to be returning to China," says the Reverend Yu Wai-Kan of the Hong Kong Church Renewal Movement, a Protestant umbrella grouping.
"Politically, our space in the future may be limited but religiously and culturally we hope it will be sufficient."
"We hope the Chinese government realises that Christians are not a threat, that we are good people, hard working, obedient and cooperative."

"Concerning the handover, we are positive but realistic. Things have been easy for us in Hong Kong under the British because Britain is a Christian country. We are going to have a more pluralistic society as part of China. We must be flexible and not take anything for granted."
Christianity came to Hong Kong on the heels of British troops in 1841, although its presence elsewhere was long established in China.

Christian missionaries played an important role in opening China up to the West, often against Beijing's will. As a result, organised religion is still regarded by some in the Chinese government as a suspect relic of the expiring colonial era.

Language in the Basic Law, promulgated by Beijing in 1990 as Hong Kong's post-handover constitution, seems to guarantee future religious freedom. But Christian activists worry incoming Chinese officials will subordinate the Law to communist political objectives.

They comment that both the Catholic church in China and the mainland's official Three-Self Protestant organisation are banned from proselytising or from expressing their faith through social action -- both common forms of religious conduct in Hong Kong.

"My great worry is that once China takes over, those individuals and organisations in Hong Kong, whose mission is to spread the word of God, will be squeezed," said one Chinese Christian activist who asked not to be identified.

"Of course we have been working underground in China for years but Hong Kong has been a vital base for proselytising, which we hope to continue and expand. Interference might be subtle but there are all kinds of indirect pressures officials could bring to bear upon us."
Hong Kong has about 380,000 Protestant and 250,000 Catholic residents but the Christian community's influence extends far beyond its proportion of the territory's total 6.4 million population.

"Fifty per cent of all primary and secondary education in Hong Kong is in the hands of Christian churches and more than 50 per cent of all social services are delivered through Church organisations," Yu of the Hong Kong Church Renewal Movement said.

Among these church institutions, most currently government funded, are more than 800 kindergarten, primary and secondary schools, universities, seminaries and Bible institutes, 13 hospitals and numerous day care, elder care and community centres.

The Hong Kong government estimates that 95 per cent of the beneficiaries of these educational and social services are non-Christian Chinese even though, for instance, many of the schools routinely include Christian religious instruction in their curriculum.

Hong Kong Christians say it would be naive to suppose this network of educational and service organisations, with its pervasive reach into the community, will not be subject to change after the handover.
Most Hong Kong Chinese families fled mainland communism and harbour bitter memories of political or religious persecution.
Beijing's violent crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square on June 4,1989 persuaded hundreds of thousands of Hong Kong Chinese to emmigrate abroad before the handover.
Christians were leaving the territory at twice the rate of the general population for a few years.
The exodus has now slowed and many Christian churches have taken a public position urging their members to stay on in Hong Kong.

"As an organisation we have asked our members to stay but that does not mean that some individuals are not still wrestling with the decision on a personal basis," said Reverend Wu of the Hong Kong Church Renewal Movement.
